REMARKABLE PENSION FRAUDS.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune
Detroit, Mich., Dec. 10.—Some months ago the Commissioner of Pensions made the discovery that, during the past few years, a large number of applications for pensions for the widows and children of deceased colored soldiers had been filed by parties residing in this city or vicinity. Many of the claims had been allowed, and the claimants had been drawing their pensions regularly. In every instance the claim was made in behalf of the heirs-at-law of some soldier who had been a member of the One Hundred and Second Regiment. Colored Volunteers, enlisted in Detroit. The claims having been proven, they were in due time allowed. Finally something transpired to lead the authorities at Washington to suspect something wrong in connection with these colored pensioners, and Special-Agent F. A. Wardell was accordingly sent here to investigate. He had been here but a few days before he obtained a mass of testimony implicating a colored man named James C. Richardson and Eugene Fecht, a German attorney. The former had acted as the claim-agent and Fecht prepared the papers. Detroit has a certain quarter known as "Kentucky," covering an area of several acres, and in that quarter the residents are almost exclusively colored people. As soon as Wardell and the local officers got their pipes well laid, they had no difficulty in opening communication with "Kentucky," and they soon learned that there were scores of colored women living in that quarter drawing pensions as widows of deceased soldiers, several of whom had been more children when the war closed. As soon as they could be placed, those women were arrested, and there are now twenty dusky damsels in the jail awaiting trial on the charge of defrauding the United States. Numerous "pensioners" filed to the Canadian town of Windsor, across the river. It appears that the originator of this wholesale scheme to defraud the Government was Richardson. He managed to secure a copy of the musterroll of the One Hundred and Second Regiment and took it to Lansing, and had the Adjutant-General give him the names of those killed in action. He would then say to a colored woman that she was entitled to a pension, and readily secure her cooperation. He would then take her to Fecht, who would prepare the papers, and they would be sent to Washington. No claim ever filed by Richardson was disallowed, so thoroughly fortified was he with manufactured evidence. Among those who applied was Richardson's wife, under an assumed name. It is estimated that he has defrauded the Government to the tune of $75,000, which sum, it was charged, was divided between Richardson, Fecht, and the colored applicants, the two men getting the larger share. The trial of the two men has been in progress in the United States Court here all the week, and resulted to night in the acquittal of Fecht and the conviction of Richardson.

BADLY CUT UP.
Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.
LOWA CITY, Ia., Dec. 10.—Two men, named Joseph Errott and C. O. Boyd, from River-

Iowa City, Ia., Dec. 10.—Two men, named Joseph Errott and C. O. Boyd, from Riverdale, a town some ten miles south of here, came to this city last evening and stopped at the Buerckle House. They are neighbors, and it seems that an old grudge existed between them. They met in the barn of the Buerckle House, where Errott had a team, when Boyd seized Errott by the whiskers, and an encounter ensued, when the latter at-

backed Boyd with a knife, cutting him perhaps fatally in the abdomen, on the arm, on his head, and ear, inflicting five fearful gashes, from which he bleed badly as he rushed along the street to Dr. Gillett's office, where he was cared for. Errott left for home in the night, but has since been arrested at Riverside, and will be brought back here to-day for examination. They met in the barn alone, and seemingly premeditated to settle their old grudge, where the encounter continued until other parties happened in and separated them.

COTA.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal., Dec. 10.—When the case of the extradited Mexican Cota came up in the Superior Court this morning, Deputy United States District-Attorney Lovell appeared and stated instructions had been received from Attorney-General Devens for the District-Attorney to represent the United States, maintain the action under the treaty, and endeavor to prevent a collision of the State with the Mexican authorities. At the request of Lovell, who desired to examine the case, a continuance was granted until next Tuesday.

LYNCHED.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal., Dec. 10.—A Belleville, Nev., dispatch says: Charles Marshall, a noted desperado, on Tuesday night last brutally murdered an inoffensive old man named Jack McCann, who was first shot and then kicked until he was dead. This morning, while the Sniper was starting with his prisoner for Aurora, the county-seat, a party of citizens rushed upon the Sheriff and his posse and forcibly took Marshall from their custody. The prisoner was then conveyed to the outskirts of the town and hanged.

ARKANSAS CITY, Ks., December 10. —4 p.m.—Payne's colony, which have been congregated here for several days, have moved out. The members are now at the territory line. They are fully armed and over four hundred strong. Lieutenant Masson, of the fourth cavalry, escorted them out. It is understood he will order them to halt and form a line across the road. CHICAGO, December 10, 4 p. m.—The jury in the criminal court, in the case of Dr. Charles Earll, after being out since 4 p. m. Wednesday, returned this morning with a verdict, pronouncing Dr. Earll guilty of the murder of Etta Carl, in attempting to produce an abortion and fixing his punishment at five years in the penitentiary. Pensions.
Special Dispatch to The Bee.

WASHINGTON, December 10—4 p. m.—The pension appropriation bill, the second of the regular series, was reported this morning by Mr. Hubbell, of Michigan. It appropriates the sum of fifty million of dollars which was the full amount recommended. The estimate of the appropriation for the current fiscal year, was $32,404,000, but the committee says it estimates that a further appropriation of $17,000,000 will be needed for the current year. The appropriation committee insert the following clause recommended by the commissioner of pensions. "The accrued pension due to Indian pensioners, shell in the discretion of the commissioners be paid in installments."

He swore they could take his wife only over his dead body. A fight ensued, and he was shot and mortally wounded by the constables.

Kelley Dethroned.

Special dispatch to The Bee.

New York, December 10, 4 p. m.—Mayor Cooper has sent to the board of aldermen, now in special meeting at City hall, the name of Alderman Allan Campbell for comptroller in place of John Kelley. The board are filibustering on the nomination, which has caused a great deal of excitement.

LATER—Allen Campbell was confirmed comproller, in place of John Kelly, by a vote of 13 to 9. Four Tammany, 5 Irving Hall and 4 republican aldermen voted in the affirmative and 5 Tammany, 2 Irving Hall and 2 republicans in the negative.

Versailles Destroyed.

Special Dispatch to The Bee.

FRANKFORT Ky., December 10—4 p. m. —Private advices from Versalles, Ky., say a most disastrous fire occurred there this morning, destroying a large part of the town. Seventeen buildings were burned including stores and dwelling houses in the heart of the town.

Sam Cole, a negro waiter, who was shot in a Chicago gambling den, died on the 11th inst. Theodore Harris, a brother waiter, on being arrested, confessed having fired the shot.

John B. Hardie, a United State deputy marshal, was killed, and Horace J. Bone, deputy collector, seriously wounded by "moonshines" in Marshall county, Ala., on the 9th inst.

Near Bellville, Nev., on the 10th inst., a mob overpowered a guard who was conducting Chas. Marshall, a noted desperade, sent to prison, for brutally murdering an inoffensive man named McCann, conveyed the prisoner to the outskirts of the town and lynched him.

At Port Oak, Texas, on the 9th inst., a party of men rode up to the store of Russell Bros., and after making purchases to the extent of $200, they commenced a fusilade on the proprietors, killing Abner Russell and probably fatally wounding his brother John.

Four negro convicts working on a plantation near Little Rock, on the 10th inst., broke from their guards. One was shot dead, but the others plunged into the cyprus swamps, and eluded the bloodhounds put on their trail.

On the 10th, two constables attempted to arrest the wife of Joseph Vance (colored) near Rock Island, Ark. Vance defended his house, and was shot dead before the arrest of his wife was effected.

A woman about 35 years old, wife of a German named Glassma, living on the Meni farm, in Marquette, Green Lake county, Wis., in a fit of temporary insanity killed her babe by cutting its head nearly off. She then went to the sheep shed and cut her own throat, dying immediately. There was jealousy between man and wife.

The dead bodies of a man and woman were found in the woods near Moscow, Ind. From the wounds in the head of each it would appear that the man murdered the woman, and then committed suicide. The identity of the parties has not been established.

A bailiff was shot dead at Cookstown, in the County of Tyrone, on the 8th, while trying to execute a decree. The party who fired the fatal shot escaped.

John Brophy and Tom Casey two well-known police officers of Louisville, Ky., who had been on bad terms for some time, met casually in a railway signal shanty on the 8th inst., and engaged in a bloody duel, the former using a revolver and Casey a dark knife. Brophy received a mortal wound in the bowels, but not until he had peppered Casey dangerously in the vicinity of the right shoulder.

In Newberry county, N. C., a shocking tragedy occurred on the 6th inst. John Lyles married a Miss Thomas of Union county several years ago. She died and he married her youngest sister, who died within a year. Lyles then married Miss Gidnau, of Newberry. James Thomas, father of the first two wives, met Lyles at Newberry, when a dispute arose about property and Thomas killed Lyles. Before Lyles fell he shot Thomas and his son. Young Thomas died on the 7th.

The little town of Gilson, Ill., is horrified at the discovery of the remains of an unknown man, well dressed, and apparently 30 years of age, in a field, with a bullet hole in his heart, a revolver, with one chamber empty, by his side, and with a drove of hogs devouring flesh off his face and hands. The coroner returned a verdict of suicide, but there was no evidence to show it was not murder, and no clew whatever was obtained to the identity of the deceased. Ed Powell and Dr. E. N. Cushing were playing cards at Trinidad, Col., on the 7th inst., and quarreled. Powell fatally shot Cushing in self-defense.

WILD WESTERN SCENES.
A Murderer Lynched.
A Murderer Lynched.
DENVER, COL., July 24.—Chas. Norton shot policeman O'Nell at Kokomo yesterday afternoon. Norton was intoxicated and was raising a disturbance in a saloon, when the policeman attempted to arrest him and was shot dead. The murderer was taken to the jail and several deputy sheriffs were placed on guard. A crowd soon gathered, over-powered the guard, and taking the prisoner out lynched him. Before he was hung he confessed to having committed other murders and said he ought to have been tung long ago.

A Female Rider's Challenge.
Miss Minnie Plenno, of Greely, has challenged the winner of a 20-mile ride at Minneapolis, to ride 10, 15 or 20 miles in Denver, St. Louis, Kansas City, Minneapolis or Chicago for $2,000 a side.

A Prisoner Drowns Himself and a Constable.
ST. PAUL, MINN., July 24.—A special from Winnipeg, Man., to the Pioneer Press says: While Constable Power was crossing Red river with Mike Carroll, an escaped prisoner, the latter upset the boat and both were drowned.

CRIMINALITIES.
A dispatch from Leadville, dated the 23d, says: Gen. Grant arrived last evening at 9:30. He was received by a company of mounted police, two companies of cavalry, five companies of infantry, city fire department and five hundred veterans of the late war. A salute of one hundred guns was fired while the procession was marching through the city. The line of march was brilliantly illuminated and decorated and streets crowded. It is said that nearly 30,000 people were on the streets. The general excused himself from making a speech on account of hoarseness. To-morrow he will visit the mines, attend the theater in the evening, and a ball and reception after the theater. The party will remain until Monday. The city expends $20,000 mostly raised by private subscription, for the entertainment.

OUTRAGEOUS SCENE IN A STREET CAR.

A dispatch from St. Joseph, dated the 19th, says: There was a shooting scrape on a street car coming from New Ulm park Sunday evening. Roughs named Bob Hughes, Jeff Tolin and Cunningham had a pass with the car driver about a fare. The driver drew a car hook and struck at Hughes who shot him in the forearm. Cunningham tried to prevent a second shooting and knocked Hughes' arm down. The revolver went off striking an infant in the arms of its mother, Mrs. Smith, wounding it in the arm, the bullet then striking the mother in the wrist and ranging up to the elbow, where it lodged. Hughes skipped, but was arrested this afternoon in Atchison. There is great excitement and threats of lynching Hughes if he comes up on the train to-night. A movement is on foot to organize a vigilance committee.

A FOUL MURDER UNEARTHED.

Workingmen excavating near the relay depot at East St. Louis, came upon a long box which contained the decomposed remains of a man, whose right arm had been broken, whose throat had been cut, and on whose head there were several wounds. Over a year ago Judge Mayo, a banker at Olney, Ill., disappeared at this depot, and it has always been thought that he was enticed from a night train on some pretext, and murdered for his money. As the body discovered by the laborers is believed to be that of Judge Mayo, his friends have been notified.

LYNCHED AND MUTILATED.

A Santa Fe dispatch of the 17th, says: A desperado named Jas. Donnegan, who was appointed on the police a few weeks ago, got drunk Wednesday night and shot Antonio Griego (Mexican), a policeman. This morning about 3 o'clock Donnegan was taken from jail, shot, mutilated and hung in an alley near the jail. Last evening the sheriff was heard to say to a Mexican in Spanish, while talking about the previous murder: "Never mind, Donnegan will be lynched to-night." The affair creates little excitement, Donnegan having no friends.

A HORSE THIEF HANGED.

A dispatch from Fort Scott, dated the 22d, says: A horse thief named Crissman was captured a few miles southeast of this city, taken by a body of masked men and hanged. During the trial he presented a certificate of deposit for $1,000 on a Kansas City bank as a bribe to the men to release him, which was refused and the man was hung after a short trial. The coroner was notified and held an inquest yesterday. The jury rendered a verdict in accordance with the facts stated. Crissman had just come from Colorado, via Kansas City.

A TERRIBLE DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.

Solomon Easterly, of Lyons, N. Y., had long been a sufferer from an ugly mother-in-law. Finally he began an action for divorce, but on the old lady promising to remain away he withdrew the suit, and thereafter lived peaceably with his wife. On Sunday the mother-in-law appeared at his house. He ordered her away but she refused to leave, and he fired at her three times. The bullets failing to take effect, he brained her and his wife with an ax, and soon after drowned himself.

TRAIN BOBBERS ARRESTED.

A dispatch from St. Joseph, dated the

22d. says: Ike Brooks and a man named Ballard were arrested in this city to-day for the train robbery at Winthrop. Ballard came up on the Council Bluffs train No. 4, and was arrested on the train by Police Officers Hillian, Eggert and Walton. A few minutes later Police Officer Donohue arrested Brooks. Both men are now in jail awaiting the action of the grand jury.

FOURTEEN PRISONERS ESCAPE FROM JAIL.

Fourteen inmates of the county jail at Burlington, Iowa, overpowered a young man whom the jailer had left in charge while he attended a picnic, and, taking to the bush, escaped. One of the men who got away is a murderer. The jail is a shabby affair, and it has been found necessary in times past to place patrolmen on the outside to prevent prisoners from breaking out.

MURDERED BY MOLLIE MAGUIRES.

A dispatch from Pottsville, Pa., dated the 22nd, says: James Wood, aged sixty, engineer of the stationary engine for the Lehigh Coal and Navigation company, was murdered last night at Bull Run, between Tamaqua and Summit Hill, by masked men. The old haunts of the Mollie Maguires have been turbulent for several days past.

GEN. GRANT ROBBED.

A dispatch from Denver, dated the 19th, says: Just before daylight this morning robbers entered the apartments of the Grant family at the Beebe house, Manitou, and stole $400 worth of jewelry and money. The robbery is supposed to have been committed by sharpers who followed the Grant party to Manitou. Mayor Bacon, of Colorado Springs, has a detective at work.

A FATAL QUARREL BETWEEN TWO FARMERS.

A dispatch from Oswego, Kan., dated the 20th, says: A fatal affray occurred near Mound Valley, in this county, yesterday, between two farmers named Watkins and Riggs, about some stock. The former shot the latter who died to-day. The murderer was arrested and is in custody. We now have three murderers in this county to deal with.

THE WINTHROP TRAIN ROBBERS.

A dispatch from St. Joseph, dated the 24, says: The case of Ballard and Brooks, Winthrop train robbers, came up in the circuit court to-day. They waived formal examination, and bail was fixed at $5,000 each. At 7 o'clock this evening bail had not been procured. The case will come up at the September term.

KILLED A POLICEMAN.

A man named Charley Norton killed a policeman in Kokomo, Col., near Leadville, on the 23d, and, soon after being placed in jail, was taken out by a mob and lynched. He admitted just before the boys swung him off that he had murdered three other men, and that the punishment was just.

A MURDEROUS MINER.

A Leadville miner threatened the life of a hardware-dealer, when his arrest was attempted. He killed two policemen and wounded a third, but was at length overpowered and locked up, with a good prospect of being lynched before morning.

SHOT AN OFFICER.

John Cone, marshal of Canfield, O., was shot and killed on the night of the 17th, by one of a gang of drunken roughs from a neighboring town. The murderer seized a hand car and escaped.

SHOT HIS NEIGHBOR IN THE BACK.

Mr. Johnson, of Abingdon, Va., rented some land from Mr. Roberts which Mr. Doan claimed to own. Doan then laid in wait for Johnson and shot him in the back, killing him.

A LOTTERY SWINDLER ARRESTED.

The police of Burlington, Iowa, have arrested a young fellow named D. N. Kratzer for conducting a lottery swindle in that city.

A DESPERATE CULPRIT.

Mr. Power, chief constable at Winnipeg, Manitoba, undertook to cross a river with a prisoner in a skiff, when the latter, a desperate fellow, upset the boat, and both drowned.

FOUND DEAD IN HIS CELL.

The marshal of Bucyrus, O., knocked a man, whom he had arrested, on the head and placed him in a cell. The next morning the prisoner was dead.

TWO NEGROES HANGED.

Two negroes were hanged at Osceola, Ark., on the 10th, in the presence of three thousand spectators, for the murder of a man of their own race.

A PENNSYLVANIA OUTLAW ARRESTED.

Harry English, an outlaw from Bradford, Pa., is under arrest at Cheboygan, Mich. Rewards aggregating $2,200 were offered for him.

Initiation of a Pittsburgh Gentleman into Western Mining Life.
Pittsburgh Dispatch.

Oil Inspector Ramsey, of this city, who was on a visit to the Far West several months ago, yesterday related to a reporter of the Dispatch an interesting story of how he attended a lynching in a Colorado town. His story is as follows:

"Wake up, Ramsey!" called out a companion of mine one morning at an early hour; "wake up or you will miss the lynching." I had gone to bed at an early hour, tired and sleepy, and had heard nothing of the murder which had been committed during the night.

"Hullo, Jim, is that you?" said I, "when does the thing take place?"

"Pretty d—d quick," answered my friend.

So, hurriedly donning my clothes, I sauntered out and found my "bunky" waiting at the door of the shanty. We walked up street a short distance, and finding a crowd of rough-looking miners around the door of a gambling hell, we pushed through and entered the saloon, where we found a Coroner's jury impaneled and about to begin their investigation. Two tables, used for dealing fare, had been pushed together, and on them was stretched the dead body of a police officer. I had known him well. He was a splendid specimen of manhood, fully six feet six six inches in height and built in proportion, a quiet inoffensive citizen, but a thoroughly good officer. On the top of the body lay a coil of half-inch rope, neatly rolled up, with a hang-man's noose at one end. As we entered the Coroner called the first witness, who, having been sworn, stated that "on the evening previous he had been in the gambling saloon of Jim Beggs, where two fellows were playing cards; during the game they quarreled about something, and both got up from the table and entered the barroom, where they both drank, and again commenced to wrangle about the bets. They made considerable noise, and in the midst of it the officer came in and quietly said, 'Boys, less noise; this must be stopped.' He had no sooner said this than one of the gamblers jerked out his 'gun' (revolver) and shot the officer through the heart." The witness had proceeded thus far, when a strapping big fellow, clad in a red flannel shirt, and with pantaloons stuck in his boot-legs, a broad-brimmed hat half hiding his dark eyes, quietly walked up to the dead body, and, taking hold of the coil of rope, said: "Boys, that's enough, come on," pushing his way out through the crowd, followed by fifteen or twenty of his companions. Without a word they walked down to the "cooler" (frame station-house), where the prisoner had been incarcerated, and, coming up to the six men on guard, demanded the keys. They told them that the keys were not in their possession.

"Hold up your hands, then," cried the leader. "Let's examine you."

The guards held up their hands and quietly submitted to the examination. The lynchers finding that the keys were not in their possession, went to a woodpile, and, picking up an ax, speedily demolished the door. The leader then entered the room and in a few minutes came out with one end of the rope over his shoulder, and, at the other end was the murderer, the noose tightly around his neck. I had taken my stand on the opposite side of the street, and could plainly see the poor devil as he came out. He was richly clad, a large diamond stud glistened on his shirt-front, and on the little finger of his left
His countenance did not betoken fear; in fact, to look at the man one would have thought the whole performance was but a joke. After reaching the street the crowd seized hold of the rope and led the victim down to an old building, where a beam jutted over the sidewalk. When they reached this point one of the number climbed out over the beam, and the end of the rope was thrown to him. After pulling the slack up he slowly let it down on the other side, and then leaned his elbows down on the beam, and took a deliberate look at the crowd below. The leader of the committee then approached the gambler and said: "Weil, Jim, yer time's short; want to say anything?"

Jim replied and said: "Now look here; can't you jist as well put a few bullets through me; what's the difference? I've got $1,000 in my pockets, and you can divide the whole thing among you if you don't hang. Will you do it?"

"Not by a d-d sight," said the leader. "You murdered a good man, and you got to swing for it."

"Well," said Jim, "go on; I suppose I must swing; this is the third man I put away, so I suppose my time's up."

He had no sooner said the words than the rope was quickly pulled up, and Jim was dangling in a horrible manner. His hands not being tied, he reached up over his head and grasped the rope, and thus released the strangulation.

"That won't do, Jim," cried the leader, and they let the dangling victim down again and speedily tied his arms behind him, and again elevated him, where he hung for nearly an hour. After it was ascertained that their victim was dead the "committee" sent for a photographer, and had a photograph taken of the entire "gang." In the foreground the committee could be seen—every face easily recognized—while just behind them was the dangling dead man, his diamonds and jewelry shining in the early morning sun, and above him sat the assistant hangman, evidently proud of his station. The entire proceedings were as quiet as could possibly be; not a word or shout could be heard. The companion of the murderer was given six hours' time to get out of town, and was most some two miles away by some of his friends, who asked him where he was going. "Oh, the boys gave me six hours to get out of town," said he, "and I am now five hours ahead of time." This was my first initiation into Western life, and I trust my last.
